[LGRA.6.7.4] **The hanging-indent form.** `let` may be written once with its
remaining bindings indented under it, one per line ([LGRA.6.1]).

**It is layout and nothing else.** The bindings of a group are the same ordered
sequence the per-line form produces — same order, same scope, same visibility,
same prohibition on forward references ([LLET.10.1], [LLET.10.6]). A group and
the equivalent per-line run **must** compile to the same artefact.

**Groups and single `let` lines may be interleaved freely** in one rule body, in
any order. A grammar restriction there would buy a reader nothing and cost a
rule nobody can remember; which form to use is style.

**`let_binding`'s tuple-form alternative is kept parseable but is not legal in
any position, hanging or per-line** ([LGRA.6.1]). A capture-bearing match binds
in `where`, never in `let` ([LREG.4.1]); a hanging group containing one is the
same compile refusal a per-line one is, not a layout question.

```{admonition} There is no ambiguity to resolve, and no new layout machinery
:class: note
**A DS expression does not span lines.** Every binding terminates in `NEWLINE`
and the grammar has no continuation or line-joining mechanism, so an indented
line after `let foo = expr` can only be another binding — there is no wrapped
expression for it to be confused with and no lookahead needed to tell them
apart.

This is a hanging indent, **not** an align-to-the-column-of-the-first-token
rule. The existing INDENT / DEDENT layout emits on any deeper indentation, which
is all this needs.

**The shape is already in the grammar.** An `emit`, `publish` or `call`
action ([LGRA.10.1]) is a statement whose first content sits on its head line,
followed by an optional indented block of more of the same ([LGRA.10.8]). This
applies that shape to `let` rather than inventing one.
```
